title: RAG vs long context: the 32K rule I use to decide
description:
Every long-context guide says the same thing: just retrieve. Past about 32,000 tokens that advice flips, and almost nobody gives you the line for when to stuff the whole corpus into context instead.

Here are the three checks I run before I write a single query. One: does the corpus fit under 32K with room to spare? Past that the model still loads everything, but it skims the middle and drops things (lost-in-the-middle plus attention-sink starvation, the real mechanism). Two: what shape is the query? A needle lookup like "what's our refund window" buried at token 140K of a 200K dump gets missed when stuffed, but retrieval pulls the 800-token chunk to the top and the model nails it. Flip the query to "summarize every change this year" and retrieval is cooked, because no single chunk holds the answer, so that one wants the whole thing in context. Three: cost, since long context repays the full prefill on every call while retrieval keeps the prompt small.

The honest limit: retrieval can grab the wrong chunk, and long context still forgets its own middle. Neither is free. The rule just tells you which failure you would rather debug.

Size, query shape, cost. The line is 32K.
